title: Dragged Disc: Macular Heterotopia & Vitreoretinal Traction
summary: The 'dragged disc' appearance is a classic clinical sign of chronic peripheral vitreoretinal traction, characterized by the temporal displacement of the optic nerve head's vascular arcades and the macula. It is most commonly associated with Retinopathy of Prematurity (ROP), FEVR, and Ocular Toxocariasis.

sections.title: Clinical Definition
sections.content: A 'dragged disc' refers to the physical displacement of the optic disc's vascular exit points and the macula (macular heterotopia) due to centripetal traction from peripheral fibrovascular membranes. This typically results in temporal straightening of the retinal vessels and an abnormally large positive Angle Kappa.

sections.title: Common Clinical Features
content: Pseudo-exotropia: Large positive Angle Kappa due to temporal macular displacement.
Temporal straightening of the superior and inferior vascular arcades.
Ectopic Macula: Often displaced temporally and sometimes superiorly.
Peripheral 'Shagreen' or white-without-pressure in ROP/FEVR.
Stretched retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) on the nasal side.
Falciform retinal folds: Often extending from the disc to the peripheral mass.

rows: Prematurity history, peripheral avascular zone, ridge.
Peripheral granuloma with tractional band to disc.
X-linked dominant (IKBKG gene), lethal in males.

sections.title: Critical Red Flags
content: Sudden decrease in vision (Threatens macular detachment or vitreous hemorrhage).
New onset of Leukocoria (White pupillary reflex).
Presence of 'Plus Disease' (Dilated/tortuous vessels) in ROP cases.
Progression of falciform folds toward the foveal center.
Total Rhegmatogenous or Tractional Retinal Detachment (Stage 4/5 ROP/FEVR).

content.explanation: FEVR, Eales disease, Toxocariasis, Coats disease, Hemoglobinopathies (Sickle Cell), Congenital Retinoschisis, Angiomatosis Retinae, K (Incontinentia Pigmenti), ET (ROP).

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup & Imaging
content: Step 1: Wide-field Fundus Photography (RetCam or Optos) to document the extent of dragging.
Step 2: Fluorescein Angiography (FA) - Look for peripheral non-perfusion and 'pruning' of vessels.
Step 3: Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) - Assess macular anatomy, dragging, and foveal schisis.
Step 4: B-Scan Ultrasonography - Rule out total RD or mass lesions (Retinoblastoma) in hazy media.
Step 5: Genetic Testing - Crucial for FEVR (LRP5/FZD4) and IP (IKBKG).

sections.title: Management Strategy
content: Laser Photocoagulation: Ablation of the peripheral avascular zone to reduce VEGF production.
Anti-VEGF Injections: Intravitreal Ranibizumab/Aflibercept/Bevacizumab as an adjunct or primary in ROP.
Scleral Buckling: To relieve circumferential traction in certain detachment patterns.
Pars Plana Vitrectomy (PPV): Required for Stage 4/5 ROP or FEVR to peel membranes and flatten the retina.
Amblyopia Management: Aggressive patching/glasses for the pseudo-strabismus and visual deprivation.

sections.title: Surgical Technique: PPV for Dragged Disc
content: 1. Lens-sparing Vitrectomy (LSV) if possible in pediatric patients.
2. Induction of Posterior Vitreous Detachment (PVD) using Triescence.
3. Segmentation and Delamination of fibrovascular membranes.
4. Relieving 'Bridge Traction' between the disc and the periphery.
5. Endolaser to the ischemic peripheral retina.
6. Air/Gas/Oil Tamponade depending on retinal stability.

sections.title: Landmark Clinical Pearls
content: Angle Kappa Pearl: The light reflex is nasal, giving an appearance of exotropia (pseudo-XT), because the fovea is pulled temporally.
Asymmetry: FEVR is often highly asymmetric; always check the 'normal' eye with FA for peripheral non-perfusion.
The 'Drag' Force: Traction is usually in the direction of the greatest peripheral ischemia.
The 'Macular Displacement' distance: In severe ROP survivors, the fovea can be dragged more than 2 disc diameters temporally.
Post-Surgical Prognosis: Visual recovery is often limited by structural foveal changes and amblyopia.

rows: Anterior displacement of the lens-iris diaphragm (ROP).

sections.title: Recent Advances
content: Artificial Intelligence (AI): Deep learning models (e.g., i-ROP) to quantify vascular tortuosity and disc dragging.
Handheld OCT: Allowing high-resolution imaging of the infant fovea in the NICU or OR.
Anti-VEGF vs. Laser: The RAINBOW and BEAT-ROP studies provide evidence for anti-VEGF efficacy in Zone 1 disease.
Gene Therapy: Emerging research for FEVR to restore the Norrin/Wnt signaling pathway.
